title: TBX Home Broadcast Station
description: A home television broadcast station on a Raspberry Pi 5, built out of a media collecting habit. Numbered channels, a real schedule, and a seek algorithm that drops you into whatever is playing right now rather than starting a file from the beginning. FastAPI and mpv over a Unix socket, a React UI driven by an IR remote, and a front panel run by an ATtiny85.
bullets: Raspberry Pi 5, 16GB - boots straight to playback; hold T for kiosk mode to manage media directly
FastAPI backend driving an mpv playback engine over a Unix socket
Seek resolves wall time against a channel schedule; no per-viewer playback state
React web UI, operated entirely by handheld IR remote
Front panel: TM1637 7-segment channel display, VS1838B IR receiver, status LEDs
ATtiny85 power controller holding a P-channel MOSFET gate, 4-state machine in 8KB
Heartbeat GPIO line lets the ATtiny cut power only after an orderly halt
Channel 99: two original games in progress, sharing one setting and continuity
Cloud tier with Stripe, OTA updates, 48 setup wizards, 30 CLI commands
360 files, 320 passing tests, 17 of 18 software phases closed

steps.title: What It Is
steps.text:
A broadcast station, not a media server. The distinction is the schedule. A media server hands you a library and waits for you to pick something; TBX decides what is on and you tune to it.
It came out of collecting media as a hobby. Past a certain size a collection stops being something you browse - there is too much of it to pick from, and scrolling a grid of everything you own is a worse experience than having something already playing. TBX is what to do with a collection once it has got to that point.
It runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of RAM and boots straight to playback. A FastAPI backend drives an mpv playback engine over a Unix socket. The web UI is React, and the whole thing is operated with a handheld IR remote. Holding T drops out of playback into a kiosk mode for managing the media directly, so adding and organizing the collection does not mean going to a terminal.
Built solo over about two years.
steps.alt: TBX web UI showing the channel grid and now-playing display

steps.title: The Seek Problem
steps.text:
The hard part of making something behave like a broadcast network is that there is no play button. If you tune to Channel 4 at 8:00 on a Tuesday, the right thing to do is join whatever is airing, partway through, exactly where it would be.
So a channel is not a playlist with a cursor. It is a schedule plus a clock. On every tune the backend resolves the current wall time against the channel's schedule, works out which item is airing and how far into it the moment falls, and seeks mpv to that offset. Nothing is stored about where a viewer left off, because a real channel does not care - it runs whether anyone is watching or not.
Two viewers tuning to the same channel see the same frame.

steps.title: Front Panel and Remote
steps.text:
The front panel is a TM1637 4-digit 7-segment display showing the channel number, a power LED that breathes slowly while the station is idle, and an amber activity LED that flashes during imports. IR comes in through a VS1838B receiver.
The interface target was that normal use never involves a keyboard - you tune, you watch, and the kiosk mode is there when you actually want to manage the collection. Color palette is dark, amber, and gunmetal, which is what the analog broadcast gear it is imitating actually looked like.
steps.alt: TBX front panel with 7-segment channel display

steps.title: Channel 99
steps.text:
Channel 99 is a hidden game console rather than a channel. Two original games are in progress for it, sharing one setting and one continuity rather than being unrelated one-offs.
This is the part of the project furthest from finished, and it is deliberately last - the station has to work as a station before the easter egg matters.

steps.title: Where the Software Stands
steps.text:
360 files and 320 passing tests across 17 closed phases.
Shipped alongside the playback system: a cloud tier with Stripe integration, an OTA update mechanism, 48 setup wizards, 30 CLI commands, and an SD card image build pipeline. Non-code deliverables done to the same phase discipline - a Kickstarter plan, a manufacturing plan, a QC checklist, a legal pack, and a launch-day playbook.
The image builds and the tests pass. What is not finished is the hardware.

steps.title: Phase 18 - The Power Controller
steps.text:
A Pi does not have a power button, and pulling the plug on a running filesystem eventually costs you the SD card. Phase 18 is the circuit that fixes that.
An ATtiny85 in an 8-pin DIP sits between the wall supply and the Pi and holds the gate of a P-channel MOSFET, so the microcontroller physically controls whether the Pi has power at all. It runs a four-state machine - OFF, STARTING, RUNNING, SHUTTING DOWN - in 8KB of flash. A button press or an IR command wakes it. Once running, it watches a heartbeat GPIO line from the Pi; when the Pi begins an orderly shutdown the heartbeat stops, the ATtiny waits out the halt, and only then opens the MOSFET.
Supporting parts: an LP2950 LDO for the always-on rail, a VS1838B IR receiver, a TM1637 display, two 3mm LEDs, a 2N2222 driving the panel, and a 1N4007 flyback diode. Currently on the breadboard.
steps.alt: ATtiny85 power controller circuit on a breadboard

steps.title: What Is Left
steps.text:
Phase 18 closes when the measured rails match the schematic, the panel behaves under all four states, and the Pi boots, halts, and boots again on command without touching the plug.
Phase 19 is the first full assembly: the TBX image on an SD card in a real Pi in an enclosure, running as one product rather than as parts on a desk.

title: Blu - A Compiled Programming Language
alt: Blu - a compiled programming language written from scratch, targeting x86-64 Linux
description: A compiled programming language built from scratch, for no reason other than finding out whether I could. Full pipeline from lexer to native x86-64 codegen, running on Linux, with closures, record types inferred from usage, a standard library, and 400+ regression tests gating every phase. Five of eighteen phases closed.
bullets: Full pipeline: lexer, parser, semantic analyzer, IR, x86-64 codegen
Emits native x86-64 assembly; runs on Linux
Forms: record types with field types inferred from usage across the call graph
Closures with environment capture across stack frames
Stdlib: JSON, CSV, binary encoding, key-value stores, process spawning, file I/O
Keywords give, show, and when in place of return, print, and if
400+ regression tests; no phase closes until all are green

steps.title: Why
steps.text:
No practical reason. I wanted to find out whether I could build a real one - not a toy interpreter, but something with a full pipeline that emits native code and can be held to the same standards as a tool you would actually use.
Blu compiles to native x86-64 assembly and runs on Linux. The compiler is written in C++.

steps.title: The Pipeline
steps.text:
Five stages: lexer, parser, semantic analyzer, IR, x86-64 codegen.
The order they were built in matters. Lexer first, made deterministic before anything depended on it. Parser next. Then semantic analysis - undefined variables, wrong argument counts, duplicate declarations - which is the layer nobody notices until it is missing and errors start surfacing as bad codegen instead of as compile errors.

steps.title: Language Design
steps.text:
Semantics were frozen early, before the standard library went in, so the language could not drift while it was being built on.
Records are called forms, and their field types are inferred from usage across the call graph rather than declared. The keywords are give for return, show for print, and when for if.
The standard library covers JSON, CSV, binary encoding, key-value arrays used as databases, process spawning, and environment variables.

steps.title: Regression Infrastructure
steps.text:
By phase 4 the test suite was the thing keeping the project honest. Several hundred regression tests organized by category, run by shell scripts that report pass rates, now past 400.
The rule is that no phase closes until every test is green. On a compiler this is not optional - a change to codegen can silently break a language feature three layers away, and without the suite you find out weeks later in a program that used to work.

steps.title: Phase 5 - Closures, and a Build That Would Not Link
steps.text:
Phase 5 added closures and forms. Closures meant environment objects, closure allocation, and a new family of IR instructions to capture variables across stack frames. Forms meant inferring field types from how they were used across the whole call graph.
Partway in, the build collapsed into a cascade of errors that pointed everywhere and nowhere. The cause was not in the new code: #include directives had been placed after the opening brace of namespace blu, so the entire standard library had been pulled inside the namespace. Every symbol resolved to the wrong place.
By the time it was found, ir_builder.cpp had accumulated duplicate function bodies and orphaned copy-paste blocks from working around symptoms of it. Rewriting the file from scratch was faster than untangling it. Each fix exposed the next one; individually all of them were small.
Closed with forms edge cases at 113/113 and closure regression at 10/10.

steps.title: Phase 6 - File I/O
steps.text:
Blu could not touch the filesystem, which put a ceiling on what could be written in it. file.read, file.write, file.append, and file.exists: four C symbols, four arity checks, four codegen entries.
The verification program wrote a file, read it back, and confirmed it existed - which is the first point at which a Blu program could do something that outlived its own process.

steps.title: What Is Left
steps.text:
Eighteen phases planned, five closed, phase six underway.
Still ahead: a map type, a garbage collector, line numbers in error messages, a formatter, a REPL, a module system, a C FFI bridge, and a platform layer.
